newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Zaire's Mobutu steps aside in veiled abdication.
newsitem.headline: Zaire's Mobutu steps aside in veiled abdication.

text.p: Zaire's ailing president, Mobutu Sese Seko, stepped aside Friday, slipping out of his capital Kinshasa and signalling the end of over three decades of highly personalized rule over Africa's third largest nation.
A cabinet statement said the government he left behind was in charge of national policy, but the veteran leader, fighting cancer and seven months of civil war, was retaining the title of president.

Government spokesman Kin-Kiey Mulumba read the statement after Mobutu left for his northern jungle palace at Gbadolite, triggering intense speculation that he was going into exile in Morocco or France.
"Field Marshal Mobutu Friday left the capital, leaving the government in charge of the conduct of national policy" in conformity with the constitution, the statement said.

"We know that, in practice, the president has ceased all intervention in the conduct of the affairs of state," it added, referring to a three-year-old transitional constitution which in reality has never been fully implemented.

"Our constitution institutes a parliamentary regime during the period of transition. The president reigns but he does not govern," the statement said, illustrating Mobutu's determination not to cede his title as head of state.
Kin-Kiey said Mobutu's emergency rule prime minister, Gen. Likulia Bolongo, was now in charge.
South Africa, whose president, Nelson Mandela, has been trying to broker a peaceful and constitutional handover of power in Zaire, expressed surprise at the statement.

It "does not fit any of the proposals on the table," one source close to Mandela's negotiating team said. South African mediators were still waiting for Mobutu's response to proposals for his outright resignation, the source added.
Laurent Kabila, whose rebels control three-quarters of the shattered, corruption-plagued nation, returned to his Lubumbashi headquarters and began an immediate meeting with his "cabinet."
Kabila has insisted that Mobutu hand power to his Alliance of Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Congo-Zaire.

But he agreed in talks with Mandela in South Africa Thursday to give Mobutu until Monday to study the proposals. Asked earlier if he would halt the rebel advance on Kinshasa, Kabila replied, "I have nothing to say about it."
It was unclear where Kabila went during the long gap between the time when he left Cape Town and when he landed in Lubumbashi.

The United States said Mobutu's departure cleared the way for peace. Rwanda, accused by Zaire of invading, together with Uganda and Burundi, in support of Kabila's rebellion, said Mobutu's departure was a matter for Zairians alone.

Speaking after a cabinet meeting, Kin-Kiey said Kisangani Archbishop Laurent Monsengwo, a key player early in Zaire's democratic transition, would negotiate with Kabila's rebels on a new transitional government and elections.

"If the parties to the conflict, in particular the rebel alliance, act in good faith, the president's important decision to stand aside, coupled with the constraints which the constitution imposes ... will allow us to find a satisfactory compromise between the positions of the belligerents," he said.

State television reported Mobutu had gone to his stronghold home region of Gbadolite on doctors' orders. "The president of the republic went to Gbadolite this morning. He will take a few days of rest on the advice of his doctors," it said.
Political and diplomatic sources said earlier that army chiefs had told him they could not defend the capital against the rebels and that he should leave for his own safety.
A Western diplomat in Morocco said Mobutu was expected there in the next 48 hours. "It seems that he has chosen Morocco as a place for exile," the diplomat said.
"I am hearing that Morocco is a likely first stop, with France as a final destination," one Western diplomat in Paris said. France, which has backed him throughout, declined all comment.

Mobutu, 66, who is reputed to have amassed a huge personal fortune as his country got poorer over the years, seized power in 1965. Western powers, ignoring the corruption of his dictatorial rule, supported him as a Cold War bastion against Soviet communism.
Kabila, 56, and histook up arms in October in a dispute over Zairian nationality for ethnic Tutsis who had lived in eastern Zaire for generations.
A close Mobutu relative said earlier that members of Mobutu's entourage were told Thursday night to pack their bags and be ready to leave Kinshasa by dawn Friday morning.
Kinshasa, a teeming city of five million people, spent its third night under curfew but a semblance of normality returned Friday on news that Mobutu was studying the peace proposal.
Mandela has been trying to avert a battle for Kinshasa but many residents were more afraid of a goodbye looting rampage by soldiers of Mobutu's notoriously ill-disciplined and usually unpaid army.
Many had feared the worst Thursday, after the collapse Wednesday of Mandela's efforts to bring Mobutu and Kabila together on a South African ship in Congo.
As reports of Mobutu's departure spread through the streets, opponents expressed cautious satisfaction.
"We are waiting now for Kabila. We hope there has been an agreement to avoid bloodshed," Blaise Bomba, a member of the unofficial opposition "street parliament," said.

Switzerland ordered a freeze on any sale of a Mobutu villa but not all his alleged assets. The government said the public prosecutor in rebel-held Lubumbashi requested a freeze of all Mobutu's assets there.
British Home (Interior) Secretary Jack Straw said the situation in Zaire had become so dangerous that people from the central African country could claim asylum.
